title: Pterygium: Masterclass in Diagnosis & Management
summary: A comprehensive clinical deep-dive into the pathogenesis, classification, and surgical management of pterygium. This guide focuses on identifying clinical activity, precise grading, and evidence-based surgical protocols to minimize recurrence.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: A pterygium is a triangular, wing-shaped fibrovascular proliferation of the subconjunctival tissue that extends onto the cornea, crossing the limbus. It is characterized by elastotic degeneration of collagen and fibrovascular proliferation, often involving a focal Limbal Stem Cell Deficiency (LSCD). Pathogenesis involves UV-B induced DNA damage, up-regulation of cytokines (VEGF, TGF-β), and matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs).

branches: Cap: Halo-like avascular zone at the leading edge
Head: Apex of the triangle, firmly attached to the cornea
Neck: The constricted portion at the limbus
Body: Fleshy portion on the bulbar conjunctiva
Fuchs' Islets: Small white spots near the head representing active precursors
Stocker’s Line: Iron deposition (haemosiderin) at the leading edge

rows: Limbus to midway between limbus and pupillary margin (<2mm)
Extends significantly across the visual axis/central cornea
Episcleral vessels clearly visible underneath the pterygium body.
Episcleral vessels partially obscured by the fibrovascular tissue.
Episcleral vessels totally obscured by the thick body. High recurrence risk.

sections.title: 6. Clinical Signs of Active Growth
content: Presence of Fuchs' Islets (active precursor spots).
Absence of Stocker's Line (Iron line indicates stability).
Marked vascular congestion and 'fleshiness' (Tan T3).
Progressive increase in induced with-the-rule (WTR) astigmatism.
Patient-reported growth over 3-6 months.

rows: Post-trauma/burn; probe can pass under the neck (negative probe test).
Leukoplakic, gelatinous, or papilliform; lacks classic wing shape.
Degeneration limited to conjunctiva; does NOT cross the limbus.
Solid, white-yellow choristoma; usually congenital and inferotemporal.

sections.title: 8. Ocular Examination & Workup
content: Step 1: Visual Acuity and Manifest Refraction (Assess induced astigmatism).
Step 2: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy (Evaluate head, neck, body, and T-grade).
Step 3: Corneal Topography (Quantify irregular astigmatism and flattening).
Step 4: Anterior Segment OCT (Measure depth of stromal invasion and thickness).
Step 5: Photography (Serial documentation for monitoring growth).

sections.title: 9. Indications for Surgical Intervention
content: Visual axis involvement (or threat to visual axis).
Induced astigmatism (>1.5D or symptomatic).
Chronic ocular irritation refractory to medical therapy.
Restriction of extraocular motility (Diplopia).
Significant cosmetic disfigurement.

rows: Obsolete due to unacceptably high recurrence.
Gold standard. Usually superior donor site.
Transfers stem cells; ideal for recurrent cases.
Used when conjunctiva must be preserved (e.g., Glaucoma).
Extensive dissection (Hirst technique); high learning curve.

sections.title: 11. Surgical Steps: CAG with Fibrin Glue
content: 1. Topical/Subconjunctival anesthesia (Lidocaine + Epinephrine).
2. Excision of the head (Smooth keratectomy).
3. Wide excision of the body and underlying Tenon's capsule.
4. Measurement of the defect (Bare sclera area).
5. Harvest superior conjunctival graft (thin, no Tenon's).
6. Application of Fibrin Glue (Tisseel/Artiss).
7. Graft placement (Ensure limbal-to-limbal orientation).

sections.title: 12. Adjuvant Therapies
content: Mitomycin C (MMC): 0.02% intraoperatively for 2-3 mins (Risk of scleral melting).
5-Fluorouracil (5-FU): Less potent than MMC; used for 'fleshy' recurrences.
Anti-VEGF (Bevacizumab): Subconjunctival injection to reduce vascularity.
Beta-Irradiation: 15-30 Gray (historical; risk of late scleral necrosis).

content.explanation: Stocker's Line (Iron present), Small Size, Sluggish growth, Sparse vasculature (Atrophic), and Symptoms (Minimal).

sections.title: 14. Post-Operative Management
content: Topical Steroids (Pred Forte 1%): Tapering over 4-8 weeks to prevent recurrence.
Topical Antibiotics (Moxifloxacin): 1 week duration.
Lubricants: Preservative-free for 3-6 months.
UV Protection: Mandatory sunglasses for all outdoor activities.

sections.title: 15. Surgical Complications
content: Graft Retraction or Loss (if glue fails).
Pyogenic Granuloma (inflammatory response).
Scleral Melting/Necrosis (secondary to MMC or radiation).
Symblepharon and Diplopia.
Cyst formation or Inclusion cysts at the graft interface.

sections.title: 16. Clinical Pearls & Landmark Wisdom
content: Always measure from the limbus, not the pupillary edge, for consistent grading.
A negative 'Probe Test' (inability to pass a probe under the neck) confirms a true Pterygium.
In recurrent cases, always check the pathology to rule out OSSN.
Fibrin glue reduces surgical time and post-op pain compared to 10-0 Nylon sutures.
The 'Limbal Stem Cell' niche must be respected; don't cauterize the limbus excessively.
